title: Massive antenna, silent mirror
caption: The retired Swedish-ESO Submillimeter Telescope under the night sky, La Silla Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at La Silla Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The great dish of the Swedish-ESO Submillimeter Telescope, SEST, mirrors the starry sky in this night view of ESO’s La Silla Observatory in Chile’s Atacama Desert. Its reflective surface is 15 meters across, and here it is tinted by airglow, a faint natural light given off by atoms high in the atmosphere.

When SEST saw first light in 1987, it was the only large submillimeter telescope in the Southern Hemisphere. It picked up light at wavelengths longer than visible light, which comes from the cold clouds of gas and dust where stars form. Signals that faint need a big collecting area to catch and sharpen, which is why telescopes like this are so large.

José Rodrigues, a visiting astronomer and photographer, took the picture. He knew the dish was 15 meters wide before he arrived, but its size still amazed him. SEST is retired now, yet it still reflects one of the darkest night skies on Earth.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph credited to J. Rodrigues/ESO. The source does not publish camera, exposure or color-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Milky Way looks brighter and more detailed here than it would to someone standing on site.

explore: Airglow happens every night, everywhere on Earth: atoms in the upper atmosphere slowly release energy they absorbed from sunlight during the day. It is usually too faint to notice except at very dark sites like La Silla.
alt: A huge telescope dish under a starry night sky, its surface reflecting a faint glow, with a person standing nearby for scale.
